section.text: Amoxicillin capsules are indicated for the treatment of infections due to susceptible (only beta-lactamase negative) isolates of the designated microorganisms. Indications include infections of the ear, nose, and throat, genitourinary tract infections, skin and skin structure infections, lower respiratory tract infections, and Helicobacter pylori eradication in combination with a proton pump inhibitor and clarithromycin. To reduce the development of drug-resistant bacteria, amoxicillin should be used only to treat infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria.

For adults and pediatric patients greater than 40 kg, the usual dose for mild to moderate infections is 250 mg every 8 hours or 500 mg every 12 hours. For severe infections, the dose is 500 mg every 8 hours or 875 mg every 12 hours. For pediatric patients 3 months and older weighing less than 40 kg, the dose is 25 to 45 mg per kg per day divided every 12 hours, or 20 to 40 mg per kg per day divided every 8 hours, depending on infection severity. In neonates and infants less than 3 months of age, the maximum recommended dose is 30 mg per kg per day divided every 12 hours. In patients with renal impairment with creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min, the dosing interval should be extended.

Amoxicillin is contraindicated in patients with a history of serious hypersensitivity reactions (anaphylaxis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome) to amoxicillin or to other beta-lactam antibacterials including penicillins and cephalosporins.

Serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reactions have been reported in patients on penicillin therapy. Before initiating therapy with amoxicillin, careful inquiry should be made regarding previous hypersensitivity reactions. Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with use of nearly all antibacterial agents, including amoxicillin, and may range in severity from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Patients with mononucleosis who receive amoxicillin develop an erythematous skin rash; amoxicillin should not be administered to patients with mononucleosis. Prolonged use may result in the overgrowth of nonsusceptible organisms.

The most frequently reported adverse reactions are diarrhea, rash, vomiting, and nausea. Hypersensitivity reactions including urticaria, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and anaphylaxis have been reported. Hematologic reactions including anemia, thrombocytopenic purpura, eosinophilia, leukopenia, and agranulocytosis have been reported during therapy with penicillins. Hepatic reactions including elevated AST or ALT and rare cases of hepatic dysfunction have been reported.

Probenecid decreases the renal tubular secretion of amoxicillin, resulting in increased and prolonged blood concentrations. Concurrent administration with allopurinol significantly increases the incidence of rashes. Amoxicillin may reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives; alternative or additional contraceptive measures should be considered. Anticoagulants such as warfarin may have their effect potentiated by amoxicillin; monitor INR more frequently.

Amoxicillin is classified as Pregnancy Category B. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Available data from published epidemiologic studies, case series, and case reports over decades have not identified an association with amoxicillin use during pregnancy and major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Amoxicillin is excreted in human milk in small quantities and is considered compatible with breastfeeding by most authorities. Dosage adjustment is required for patients with severe renal impairment.

Amoxicillin is stable in the presence of gastric acid and may be given without regard to meals. Absorption is rapid and oral bioavailability is approximately 75 to 90 percent. Peak plasma concentrations occur 1 to 2 hours after administration. The elimination half-life of amoxicillin in healthy adults with normal renal function is approximately 1 to 1.3 hours. Approximately 60 percent of an orally administered dose is excreted unchanged in the urine within 6 to 8 hours. The half-life is prolonged in patients with renal impairment.
